title: FDA Approves Updated COVID-19 Vaccines for 2026-27 Season
excerpt: Four shots from Moderna, Pfizer-BioNTech, and Novavax-Sanofi cleared for older adults and high-risk individuals as fall vaccination campaign prepares to launch.
body:
• The FDA approved updated COVID-19 vaccines from Moderna, Pfizer-BioNTech, and Novavax-Sanofi for the 2026-27 season, targeting current dominant variants.
  • Moderna's two mRNA vaccines target the XFG subvariant, Pfizer-BioNTech's Comirnaty targets LP.8.1, and Novavax-Sanofi's protein-based Nuvaxovid targets the broader JN.1 strain.
  • The vaccines are approved for adults 65 and older and those ages 5-64 with underlying health conditions — a narrower scope than previous universal recommendations.
  • Shots are expected to reach pharmacies and doctors' offices by September, though the CDC has yet to issue an official recommendation for the 2026-27 season.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved updated COVID-19 vaccines from all three major manufacturers on Wednesday, clearing the way for a fall vaccination campaign as coronavirus case counts show signs of a seasonal uptick.

Moderna, Pfizer-BioNTech, and Novavax-Sanofi each announced their vaccines had received FDA approval, following a May advisory committee vote that recommended targeting the XFG variant — the dominant strain circulating in the United States — for the 2026-27 immunization season.

What's Been Approved

Four COVID-19 shots are now approved for the new season. Moderna received clearance for its two mRNA-based vaccines: Spikevax, approved for people ages 6 months through 64 with underlying conditions and all adults 65 and older, and mNexspike, approved for those ages 12 through 64 with underlying conditions and everyone 65 and older. Both target the XFG subvariant of the JN.1 coronavirus strain.

Pfizer and BioNTech's mRNA vaccine Comirnaty was approved for all adults 65 and older and anyone ages 5 through 64 with conditions that raise their risk of severe illness. Notably, it targets the LP.8.1 strain rather than XFG.

Novavax-Sanofi's Nuvaxovid, the only protein-based COVID vaccine available in the U.S., received approval for everyone 65 and older and those 12 through 64 with underlying conditions. It targets the broader JN.1 strain.

A Narrower Recommendation

Under the Trump administration, the federal government shifted from a universal COVID vaccine recommendation to a more restricted approach. Rather than recommending vaccination for everyone, the current guidance advises all individuals 6 months and older to consult with a healthcare provider before getting the shot.

Health conditions that may raise the risk of severe illness include asthma, heart disease, kidney disease, liver disease, lung disease, diabetes, obesity, and pregnancy, according to the CDC.

Rising Case Numbers

While COVID case numbers are not especially high and the U.S. is not recording many hospitalizations or deaths, the virus continues to circulate. CDC data shows the test positivity rate for the week ending August 15 approached 5% for the first time since early February, with numbers climbing in every state.

As of early July, XFG.1.1 was the predominant coronavirus strain causing illness in the country, though the CDC has acknowledged that sequencing data has become limited due to low submissions from state and local health departments.

What Comes Next

The CDC has yet to make an official recommendation for this year's vaccines, but most major medical organizations recommend getting one. Insurance companies have indicated they will continue to cover the shots.

Experts say the updated vaccines should begin arriving at pharmacies and doctors' offices in September. The May advisory committee vote — in which eight of nine experts supported targeting XFG — followed extensive review of circulating strain data and immunogenicity studies from all three manufacturers.

For Indian Americans, particularly older adults and those with chronic health conditions prevalent in South Asian populations such as diabetes and heart disease, the updated vaccines represent an important tool heading into fall and winter respiratory season.
